note: Contracted capacity that supplies US data centers: one row per deal, each read off a public page and recorded by hand. This is the *contract* answer to where data-center power comes from, and it is deliberately not the physical one — a signed nuclear PPA does not mean nuclear electrons reach that building, it means somebody bought that attribute. The page renders this table beside the EIA generator table and shows the gap. Rules for adding a row, in order of importance. (1) One deal, one row, from the original announcement where one exists: a company press release, an IR deck, a filing, a regulator's docket, or major media quoting one of those. Never a paywalled note, never an aggregator's summary when the original is reachable. (2) `mw` is what was disclosed. If no capacity was disclosed, leave it null and say so in `caveat`; a guess, a midpoint of a range, or a figure inferred from a dollar amount is not a disclosure. A range is the lower bound in `mw` with the range written out in `caveat`. (3) `stage` is the same five-word vocabulary the EIA generator table uses (config.STAGE_ORDER), so the two tables can be read against each other; a memorandum of understanding is `announced`, not `permitted`. (4) `path` is a key of config.PATHS, the supply path the deal buys from. (5) `company_confirmed` is true only when the buyer or the seller said it themselves. Reported-but-unconfirmed deals are welcome and are flagged on the page, not hidden. (6) `caveat` is one or two sentences written for a reader, in the voice of the page: what this number is not. Every row needs one. (7) `last_checked` is the day somebody last opened `source_url` and confirmed the row still matches it; after config.REFERENCE_STALE_DAYS days the page greys the row. Re-reading the source and bumping this date is the maintenance job. (8) Never delete a row because its source went offline or the deal fell through — record the collapse as a new row or in the caveat; the page shows what was announced and what became of it. Working notes go in `curator_notes`, which pipelines/power/reference.py strips before anything can publish it; any other field containing a marker from WORKING_NOTE_MARKERS in that module is rejected outright.

rows.technology: Three new combined-cycle combustion turbine plants
rows.caveat: The 2,260 MW is the combined nameplate capacity of three utility-owned plants Entergy will build on its own system, not a block of capacity sold to Meta under a contract; Entergy has not disclosed how much of the output Meta pays for or on what terms. The Louisiana Public Service Commission approved the certification in August 2025, which is why the row is marked permitted rather than announced.
rows.curator_notes: MW figure is from Entergy's December 2024 announcement. The separate Entergy release of 2025-08-20 (entergy.com/news/entergy-louisiana-receives-lpsc-approval-for-major-infrastructure-investments-to-support-metas-data-center-and-improve-reliability) confirms LPSC approval and 1,500 MW of solar procurement authority but does not restate the gas MW.

rows.technology: Combined-cycle gas plant (Delta Blues Advanced Power Station)
rows.caveat: Entergy names no data-center customer in this release, so the link to any specific hyperscaler is reporting rather than disclosure. The 754 MW is the plant's rating, serving Entergy Mississippi's whole system; no contracted volume to a data center has been published.
rows.curator_notes: Widely reported as the generation tied to AWS's Madison County campus under Mississippi's 2023 pre-certification statute, but Entergy's own release does not say so. Keep company_confirmed false until Entergy or AWS states it.

rows.technology: Seven GE Vernova gas turbines on a former coal site
rows.caveat: This is a generation build, not a signed supply contract: no data-center tenant or offtaker is named, and "up to 4.5 GW" is the planned plant capacity rather than capacity anybody has agreed to buy. First turbine deliveries were expected to begin in 2026.
rows.curator_notes: Developer is Homer City Redevelopment with Kiewit as constructor; site is the 1,884 MW former Homer City coal plant retired in 2023. Trade coverage in April 2026 reported a 'first steel' milestone, which supports under_construction.

rows.technology: Gas redevelopment of the former Bruce Mansfield coal plant
rows.caveat: No capacity was disclosed for the new Shippingport plant, so this row carries no megawatt figure. The only capacity numbers in the announcement are the 2.7 GW rating of the retired coal plant and a statement that more than one gigawatt of surplus would go back to PJM; the co-located data-center partner is unnamed.
rows.curator_notes: EQT is named as intended gas supplier, National Fuel as pipeline. Do not treat the 2.7 GW coal rating as the new plant's size.

rows.technology: Restart of Three Mile Island Unit 1 (Crane Clean Energy Center)
rows.caveat: The 835 MW is the carbon-free energy Constellation says the restart would add to the grid, not a metered flow to any Microsoft building; the unit last operated at 837 MW before its 2019 shutdown. Restart depends on regulatory approvals and grid work, and the plant was still not generating as of this check.
rows.curator_notes: Constellation's 2025-09-23 update says the restart target moved forward to 2027 and the site is roughly 80% staffed; that page timed out on fetch, so the 2024 release is the cited source.

rows.technology: Restart of the Duane Arnold Energy Center boiling water reactor
rows.caveat: The plant has been shut down since 2020 and nothing is being delivered yet; NextEra targets grid delivery by the first quarter of 2029. The 615 MW is the unit's rating, and Google is one of two buyers named, with a rural cooperative taking the remainder.
rows.curator_notes: Central Iowa Power Cooperative takes the balance of output. Restart needs NRC action and DOE loan support reported separately.

rows.technology: Fleet of Gen IV fluoride salt-cooled advanced reactors
rows.caveat: This is a master plant development agreement setting up a path to 500 MW by 2035, not a set of executed power purchase agreements; individual PPAs and sites were left to be signed later. No state or specific plant was named at announcement.
rows.curator_notes: First deployment targeted 2030. The TVA Hermes 2 PPA of August 2025 is the first project under this framework and is recorded as a separate row.

rows.technology: Hermes 2 advanced reactor demonstration plant
rows.caveat: TVA, not Google, is the contracting purchaser; Google takes the clean-energy attributes and the power reaches its Tennessee and Alabama data centers through TVA's grid. The 50 MW is an "up to" figure from a demonstration reactor that is not yet generating, with operations expected in 2030.
rows.curator_notes: First deployment under the 2024 Google-Kairos master agreement. Hermes 2 holds an NRC construction permit and has broken ground, but stage is left at announced because no source opened this session establishes the construction status.

rows.technology: Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled small modular reactors
rows.caveat: The 320 MW is the four-unit first project with Energy Northwest, the only sized commitment in the announcement; the wider "more than 5 gigawatts by 2039" is a collaboration target with no projects or contracts attached. Amazon's role here is partly equity: it anchored a roughly $500 million financing round.
rows.curator_notes: Project carries an option to expand to twelve units and 960 MW.

rows.technology: Aurora powerhouse fast reactors
rows.caveat: Oklo describes this as a non-binding master power agreement running through 2044, with binding PPAs to follow as milestones are met, so the 12 GW is an ambition rather than contracted capacity. No sites, dates or first-project size were named, and Oklo had no reactor in operation at announcement.
rows.curator_notes: Largest headline number in the table by a wide margin; the non-binding qualifier is the whole story of this row.

rows.technology: Aurora powerhouse fast reactors
rows.caveat: Meta states "up to 1.2 GW" at a Pike County, Ohio site with power as early as 2030, so the figure is a ceiling on a project that has not been licensed or built. Oklo had no operating reactor when this was announced.
rows.curator_notes: One of three awards out of Meta's December 2024 nuclear RFP; the other two are separate rows.

rows.technology: Natrium sodium-cooled reactors with integrated thermal storage
rows.caveat: The 2.8 GW is baseload generation capacity across a multi-unit programme stretching to 2035, separate from 1.2 GW of built-in storage; only up to 690 MW has a near-term delivery date, as early as 2032. No sites were named and no Natrium unit is operating.
rows.curator_notes: Meta's wording: up to 690 MW of firm power as early as 2032, plus up to six further Natrium units producing 2.1 GW targeted by 2035.

rows.technology: Small modular reactor at the North Anna site
rows.caveat: A memorandum of understanding to explore feasibility, with no capacity, price or commitment to build disclosed by either company. Figures of at least 300 MW circulate in coverage of Amazon's wider SMR programme but do not appear in this joint announcement.
rows.curator_notes: Dominion's release stresses the RFP is not a commitment to build. Left mw null deliberately rather than importing the 300 MW from Amazon's own sustainability page.

rows.technology: Coal and oil units kept online under reliability-must-run terms
rows.source_name: Talen Energy press release filed with the SEC
rows.caveat: No data center is a party to this: it is a settlement among Talen, PJM, Maryland regulators and others that keeps Brandon Shores and H.A. Wagner running to 31 May 2029 while Baltimore-area transmission is upgraded. Talen disclosed the payment rates, $312/MW-day and $137/MW-day, but not the megawatts covered, so the capacity field is left empty.
rows.curator_notes: FERC approved the settlement in May 2025. Coverage puts the two plants at roughly 2 GW combined; that number is not in Talen's release, so it is not used here.

rows.technology: Coal units at Plants Bowen and Scherer kept in operation
rows.caveat: This is a state resource-plan approval, not a contract with any data center: the 4,000 MW is the capacity of coal units whose operation is extended through at least 2034, and none of it is assigned to a named customer. Georgia Power's own filings note its data-center load forecasts carry significant potential for overestimation.
rows.curator_notes: Same order approved up to 4,000 MW of renewables by 2035, more than 1,500 MW of storage, 268 MW of gas at Plant McIntosh and 54 MW of Vogtle uprates. Only the deferred-retirement element belongs in path A4.

rows.technology: Behind-the-meter gas turbines co-located with the data center
rows.source_name: Chevron press release filed with the SEC
rows.caveat: Chevron describes 2.67 GW of behind-the-meter power under a 20-year agreement, but the plant is not built and a final investment decision was still expected by the end of 2026. The capacity is to be phased in modules rather than delivered at once.
rows.curator_notes: Known as Project Kilby, developed with Engine No. 1; majority GE Vernova 7HA turbines with additional Solar Turbines units. The 8-K exhibit is a quarterly highlights release, dated 2026-07-31, that restates the 2026-06-22 announcement.

rows.technology: 29 LM2500XPRESS aeroderivative gas turbine packages
rows.caveat: This is an equipment order, not a power contract, and GE Vernova gave only a rounded figure, "nearly 1 GW" across the 29 units, so no capacity is recorded here. No site or state is named in the announcement, and the two tranches were booked in December 2024 and June 2025.
rows.curator_notes: The first ten units are generally associated with the Abilene, Texas Stargate campus, where Crusoe holds a Texas air permit for roughly 360 MW of on-site simple-cycle generation. That permit was not opened for this row, so Abilene is not asserted in the published fields.

rows.technology: 15 Solar SMT-130 gas turbines at the Colossus site
rows.source_name: TechCrunch, reporting the Shelby County Health Department permit
rows.caveat: The 247 MW is the ceiling written into an air permit, not a contracted supply or a measured output, and the permit treats the units as backup with strict annual run-hour limits. xAI has published nothing itself, and the permit was under appeal by community groups.
rows.curator_notes: Permitting authority is the Shelby County Health Department; the permit runs to January 2027 and required best available control technology by 2025-09-01. Aerial surveys in April 2025 counted far more turbines on site than were permitted at the time.

rows.technology: Distributed gas turbines supplying primary on-site power
rows.source_name: Solaris Energy Infrastructure press release filed with the SEC
rows.caveat: Solaris names only "a major data center client" and no site or state, so the buyer side of this row is a description rather than a name. The roughly 900 MW is the upsized contract size, up from 500 MW, over an initial seven-year term, and the equipment was still being delivered.
rows.curator_notes: The parties formed Stateline Power, LLC, owned 50.1% by Solaris. A $550 million senior secured facility supports the joint venture.

rows.technology: Solid oxide fuel cells co-located at data-center sites
rows.caveat: The gigawatt is the ceiling of a supply agreement, not equipment ordered: only 100 MW was firmly ordered at announcement, with further orders left to 2025. AEP is a utility buying the hardware, so the eventual data-center customers were not named and no site or state was given.
rows.curator_notes: Described at the time as the largest commercial fuel-cell procurement to date.

rows.technology: Solid oxide fuel cells for on-site data-center power
rows.caveat: The 1.2 GW is the portion actually contracted and being deployed; the headline 2.8 GW is what Oracle "intends to procure" under a master services agreement and is not itself an order. Bloom names no individual sites beyond saying the projects are in the United States.
rows.curator_notes: Builds on a July 2025 collaboration and an October 2025 warrant issued to Oracle. Range handled by putting the contracted lower figure in mw.

rows.technology: Solid oxide fuel cells for AI data-center campuses
rows.caveat: The only number attached to this partnership is an investment commitment of up to $5 billion, so no fuel-cell capacity is recorded; dollars are not megawatts. The scope is global rather than United States only, and the first named site under discussion was in Europe.
rows.curator_notes: Bloom and Brookfield said in 2026 they were expanding the framework to $25 billion. That expansion is a separate announcement and would be its own row.

rows.technology: Long-duration CO2 battery storage
rows.caveat: A global commercial framework with a strategic investment attached, carrying no disclosed capacity, no named projects and no United States site at announcement. Storage shifts energy in time rather than adding supply, so nothing here is new generation for a data center.
rows.curator_notes: Google's first long-duration storage commercial agreement. The Salt River Project project announced in June 2026 is the first United States deployment and is recorded separately.

rows.technology: 19 MW, 10-hour CO2 battery at the Coronado Generating Station
rows.caveat: Google's role is cost-sharing to help a utility adopt non-lithium storage, not an offtake agreement, and the output is dispatched by Salt River Project onto its grid rather than routed to a Google building. The project is small by data-center standards and is not expected online until 2029.
rows.curator_notes: Structured as a 20-year tolling agreement with Energy Dome owning and operating.

rows.technology: Second-life EV battery microgrid with solar
rows.caveat: At 12 MW and 63 MWh this powers a modular container-scale deployment, not a hyperscale campus, and the batteries store solar output rather than generate. The companies describe it as the largest second-life battery installation of its kind, which is a claim about reuse rather than about scale.
rows.curator_notes: Sited at Redwood's Sparks, Nevada campus powering Crusoe Spark modular units. The companies said in March 2026 they were expanding from 4 to 24 units.

rows.technology: Existing nuclear output from the Susquehanna plant
rows.source_name: Talen Energy press release filed with the SEC
rows.caveat: Nothing new is built here: Susquehanna already runs, and the agreement re-papers an existing 2.5 GW plant's output as a front-of-meter supply to Amazon through 2042. The full 1,920 MW is not flowing today, with the ramp expected to complete no later than 2032.
rows.curator_notes: Replaces the March 2024 behind-the-meter arrangement that came with Amazon's purchase of the Cumulus campus. Talen acts as retail supplier once transmission reconfigurations complete, expected spring 2026.

rows.technology: Existing nuclear output from the Clinton Clean Energy Center
rows.caveat: This buys the output of a plant that already exists and keeps it running after Illinois ratepayer credits expire; deliveries do not begin until June 2027. Only 30 MW of the total is new energy, coming from planned uprates.
rows.curator_notes: Constellation frames the deal as a market replacement for the state zero emission credit programme.

rows.technology: Existing nuclear output from the Comanche Peak plant
rows.source_name: World Nuclear News, quoting Vistra's fourth-quarter 2025 results call
rows.caveat: Vistra's own filing of 29 September 2025 described the counterparty only as a large investment-grade company; the chief executive named Amazon Web Services months later on an earnings call. The 1,200 MW is an "up to" figure from an existing plant, with deliveries beginning in the fourth quarter of 2027 and reaching full volume by 2032.
rows.curator_notes: The anonymous 8-K is at sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1692819/000119312525221774/d43667d8k.htm and carries the MW, term and ramp; the WNN piece is cited because it is where the buyer is named by the seller.

rows.technology: Existing nuclear output from the Perry and Davis-Besse plants
rows.caveat: Meta describes "more than 2.1 GW" from two plants that already operate, so the figure here is the lower bound of that phrasing; Vistra later put the contracted total at 2,176 MW. A further 433 MW of uprates across Perry, Davis-Besse and Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania is contracted separately and is not counted in this row.
rows.curator_notes: One of three awards from Meta's nuclear RFP. The uprate tranche is expected online in the early 2030s and could justify its own row once a source states its terms.

rows.technology: New wind and solar capacity under a global framework
rows.caveat: The 10.5 GW spans the United States and Europe, so only part of it belongs to American data centers, and it is a five-year framework for development rather than a set of signed project contracts. Capacity is meant to be delivered between 2026 and 2030, with no projects named at announcement.
rows.curator_notes: The parties describe potential extension to Asia-Pacific, India and Latin America. This is the only row in the table whose headline number is not United States specific.

rows.technology: Solar and wind power purchase agreements
rows.caveat: These are grid-connected projects in Ohio, Arkansas and Texas whose output Meta buys on paper; the electricity does not travel to a particular building, and the sites do not sit next to Meta's data centers. None was operating at announcement, with commercial operation expected in 2027 and 2028.
rows.curator_notes: Four projects: Yellow Wood 300 MW and Pleasant Prairie 140 MW in Ohio, Decoy 155 MW in Arkansas, Seaway Wind 196 MW in Texas. Brings the Meta-Invenergy total to 1,800 MW.

rows.technology: Enhanced geothermal generation at Cape Station
rows.caveat: Deliveries are not expected until 2028 from a project still being drilled, and an optional expansion of roughly 600 MW is not contracted. Enhanced geothermal at this scale has no long operating record, so the 396 MW is a contracted volume rather than demonstrated output.
rows.curator_notes: Same release was filed as an 8-K exhibit at sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001853868/000162828026059707/exhibit991pressrelease9126.htm.

rows.technology: Enhanced geothermal supplied through the Clean Transition Tariff
rows.caveat: Google does not buy this power directly: NV Energy takes the geothermal output from Fervo's Corsac Station project and Google pays a tariff premium covering the gap against the cheaper resource the utility would otherwise have built. Nevada regulators approved the structure in May 2025 and the plant was not yet generating.
rows.curator_notes: Announced June 2024, approved by the Public Utilities Commission of Nevada on 2025-05-13. Stage set to permitted on the strength of that approval. Google's data centers are in Storey County.

rows.technology: Water-independent next-generation geothermal
rows.caveat: The 150 MW is split across two phases, a small first phase and a larger second one, with both only projected to be operational by 2030 and neither sized publicly. Power goes onto the PNM grid rather than to a Meta facility directly, and XGS had no plant of this size in operation.
rows.curator_notes: XGS later brought in Baker Hughes to help advance the project.

rows.technology: Co-located renewables and storage in industrial energy parks
rows.caveat: No capacity was disclosed, only an intention to build gigawatts of co-located data-center and clean-power capacity, so this row carries no megawatt figure. Google's role is described as anchor offtaker plus investor, and no site, state or first-project size was named.
rows.curator_notes: Announced alongside a funding round into Intersect led by TPG Rise Climate and Google. First co-located project was expected partly operational in 2026 and complete in 2027.
